## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup

plink_path <- unname(Sys.which("plink"))

if (!nzchar(plink_path)) {
  stop("PLINK was not found on PATH.")
}

system2(plink_path, args = "--version")
```

```{r}
#| label: resusable-run-plink-function

run_plink <- function(
    input, 
    operation,
    output,
    input_flag = "--file"
){
  dir.create(
    dirname(output),
    recursive = TRUE,
    showWarnings = FALSE
  )
  
  status <- system2(
    plink_path,
    args = c(
      input_flag, shQuote(input),
      operation,
      "--out", shQuote(output)
    )
  )
  
  if (status != 0){
    stop(
      "PLINK failed, check the output above and ", output, ".log")
  }
  
  invisible(status)
}
```

## Exercise 1: Inspect the input files

```{r}
#| label: inspect-input-files

input_files <- c(
  "data/raw/data1.map",
  "data/raw/data1.ped",
  "data/raw/data2.tfam",
  "data/raw/data2.tped"
)

for (path in input_files){
  cat("\n--", basename(path), "--\n")
  cat(
    readLines(
      path,
      n = 5, 
      warn = FALSE,
    ),
    sep = "\n"
  )
  cat("\n")
}
```

## Exercise 2: Calculate allele frequencies in dataset 1

```{r}
#| label: allele-frequencies-data1

run_plink(
  "data/raw/data1",
  "--freq",
  "results/data1_freq"
)

freq_data1 <- read.table(
  "results/data1_freq.frq",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

cat("Allele frequencies in dataset 1")
freq_data1
```

**Interpretation**

Allele frequencies were calculated using founders with nonmissing genotypes. C at SNP1 and G at SNP3 each had a minor allele frequency of 33.33% (8 of 24 counted allele copies). At SNP2, A had a slightly higher minor allele frequency of 34.62% (9 of 26 copies). The different numbers of counted allele copies indicate that genotype availability differed between markers. All three markers were polymorphic, with both alleles present among the counted founders.

## Exercise 3: Association test in dataset 1

```{r}
#| label: association-data1

run_plink(
  "data/raw/data1",
  "--assoc",
  "results/data1_assoc"
)

assoc_data1 <- read.table(
  "results/data1_assoc.assoc",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

print("Allelic association test in dataset 1")
assoc_data1
```

**Interpretation**

The allelic chi-square tests detected no statistically significant association between the three markers and case/control status (all P \> 0.05). Although A1 frequencies were slightly higher in cases than controls, the odds ratios were close to 1 (1.111–1.224). These results do not establish that an association is absent, particularly given the small dataset. Interpretation is also limited because the basic test does not account for relationships between individuals.

## Exercise 4: Transmission disequilibrium test in dataset 1

```{r}
#| label: tdt-dataset1

run_plink(
  "data/raw/data1",
  "--tdt",
  "results/data1_tdt"
)

tdt_data1 <- read.table(
  "results/data1_tdt.tdt",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)

print("Transmission disequilibrium tests in dataset 1")
tdt_data1
```

**Interpretation**

The TDT detected no evidence of preferential allele transmission to affected offspring at any of the three markers. Transmitted and untransmitted counts were equal at SNP1 (1:1), SNP3 (2:2) and SNP2 (3:3), resulting in odds ratios of 1, chi-square statistics of 0 and P-values of 1. These findings agree with the lack of significant association in Exercise 3, although the tests examine different comparisons. The small number of informative transmissions possibly limits the power to detect an association.

## Exercise 5: Fisher's exact test in dataset 1

```{r}
#| label: fisher-data1

run_plink(
  "data/raw/data1",
  c("--assoc", "fisher"),
  "results/data1_fisher"
)

fisher_data1 <- read.table(
  "results/data1_fisher.assoc.fisher",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

print("Fisher’s exact association tests in dataset 1")
fisher_data1
```

**Interpretation**

Fisher’s exact tests detected no statistically significant association between the three markers and case/control status (P = 0.8224–0.8350). Allele frequencies and odds ratios matched those from Exercise 3, while the P-values differed because of the testing method. Both methods therefore lead to the same conclusion: these data provide insufficient evidence of allelic association. Fisher’s test does not resolve the limitation that individuals in this dataset are related.

## Exercise 6: Linkage disequilibrium between SNP1 and SNP2

```{r}
#| label: ld-data1-snp1-snp2

run_plink(
  "data/raw/data1",
  c("--ld", "SNP1", "SNP2"),
  "results/data1_ld_snp1_snp2"
)

ld_log <- readLines(
  "results/data1_ld_snp1_snp2.log",
  warn = FALSE
)
```

**Interpretation**

SNP1 and SNP2 showed complete linkage disequilibrium among the analyzed founders (r\^2 = 1, D' = 1). The estimated haplotypes were C–A (33.33%) and T–G (66.67%), while T–A and C–G had approximately zero frequencies. These estimates indicate perfect prediction between the markers in this sample. The finding does not establish that perfect LD exists in the wider population or that recombination has never occurred between them.

## Exercise 7: Missing data in dataset 1

```{r}
#| label: missing-data1

run_plink(
  "data/raw/data1",
  "--missing",
  "results/data1_missing"
)

missing_individuals <- read.table(
  "results/data1_missing.imiss",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

missing_markers <- read.table(
  "results/data1_missing.lmiss",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  missing_markers,
  caption = "Missing genotypes per marker"
)

knitr::kable(
  missing_individuals[missing_individuals$N_MISS > 0, ],
  caption = "Individuals with at least one missing genotype"
)
```

**Interpretation**

Missing-data analysis identified 22 missing genotype calls out of 165 (13.33%) across 55 individuals and three markers. SNP1 had the highest missingness (20.00%), followed by SNP3 (10.91%) and SNP2 (9.09%). Eleven individuals had at least one missing genotype, including five with no genotype data at any marker. Missing genotypes reduce the information available for analysis and can cause the contributing sample to differ between markers.

## Exercise 8: Relevant quality control steps for genotyping-platform data and options provided by PLINK

Relevant quality control steps for genotyping-platform data checks both the individuals and the markers, because unreliable genotypes can distort association results. The following is a list of those steps, for which PLINK also offers some options:

- **Missing genotypes per individual**: Identify samples with poor genotyping success
- **Missing genotypes per marker**: Identify markers that frequently fail
- **Minor allele frequency**: Identify variants with too few minor allele copies for the intended analysis
- **Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (HWE)**: Flag unusual genotype proportions that may indicate errors or population structure
- **Mendelian errors**: Detect genotypes inconsistent with recorded parent–offspring relationships
- **Unusual heterozygosity**: Investigate possible contamination, inbreeding or other sample problems
- **Recorded sex consistency**: Investigate discrepancies using suitable sex-chromosome data
- **Duplicates and relatedness**: Identify duplicate samples or unexpected relatives
- **Population structure**: Identify ancestry differences that could confound association tests

## Exercise 9: Allele frequencies in dataset 2

```{r}
#| label: allele-frequencies-data2

run_plink(
  "data/raw/data2",
  "--freq",
  "results/data2_freq",
  "--tfile"
)

freq_data2 <- read.table(
  "results/data2_freq.frq",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

print("Allele frequencies in dataset 2")
freq_data2
```

**Interpretation**

All eight markers were polymorphic, with minor allele frequencies ranging from 8.33% at SNP7 to 50.00% at SNP6. Each marker had 24 counted allele copies, corresponding to 12 founders with non-missing diploid genotypes. SNP7’s minor allele was represented by only two copies, providing limited information for association testing. At SNP6, both alleles were equally frequent.

## Exercise 10: Association test in dataset 2

```{r}
#| label: association-data2

run_plink(
  "data/raw/data2",
  "--assoc",
  "results/data2_assoc",
  "--tfile"
)

assoc_data2 <- read.table(
  "results/data2_assoc.assoc",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

assoc_data2$P_BONF <- p.adjust(
  assoc_data2$P,
  method = "bonferroni",
  n = 8
)

print("Allelic association tests in dataset 2")
assoc_data2
```

**Interpretation**

Allelic chi-square tests identified nominal associations at SNP5 (P = 0.01298) and SNP6 (P = 0.01431). A at SNP5 was less frequent in cases than controls (OR = 0.10), whereas C at SNP6 was more frequent in cases (OR = 9.00). Neither association remained significant after Bonferroni correction for eight tests (threshold = 0.00625). Given the small sample and low allele counts, these results should be compared with Fisher’s exact tests.

## Exercise 11: Fisher's exact test in dataset 2

```{r}
#| label: fisher-data2

run_plink(
  "data/raw/data2",
  c("--assoc", "fisher"),
  "results/data2_fisher",
  "--tfile"
)

fisher_data2 <- read.table(
  "results/data2_fisher.assoc.fisher",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

fisher_data2$P_BONF <- p.adjust(
  fisher_data2$P,
  method = "bonferroni",
  n = 8
)

print("Fisher’s exact association tests in dataset 2")
fisher_data2
```

**Interpretation**

Fisher’s exact tests identified nominal associations at SNP5 (P = 0.03607) and SNP6 (P = 0.03913), consistent with the unadjusted conclusions from the chi-square tests. Neither remained significant after Bonferroni correction for eight markers (adjusted P = 0.28856 and 0.31304, respectively). The remaining markers showed no significant association. Thus, no marker met the significance criterion after accounting for multiple testing.
